q: What do we call a baby shark?
why: Baby sharks are called pups, just like young seals and dogs. Many pups swim off on their own right after birth.
hint: Think of a word we also use for a young dog.

q: A whale is a kind of fish.
why: Whales are mammals. They breathe air through lungs, feed milk to their calves, and must come up to the surface to breathe.
hint: Do whales breathe air or water?

q: Which dinosaur had three horns on its face?
why: Triceratops means 'three-horned face.' Stegosaurus had plates on its back, and Brachiosaurus had a very long neck.
hint: The first part of the name is a number word.

q: How many legs does a spider have?
why: Spiders have 8 legs. Insects have only 6, so a spider is not an insect.
hint: Count the pairs: there are four pairs.

q: Which body part fills with air when you breathe in?
why: Lungs take in air and give your body oxygen. Your stomach holds food, and your heart pumps blood.
hint: You breathe with them inside your chest.

q: Which planet is the biggest one in our solar system?
why: Jupiter is so big that more than a thousand Earths could fit inside it. Mars is smaller than Earth.
hint: It is a giant gas planet.

q: Put the day in order, as the Sun moves across the sky.
why: The Sun comes up in the morning, is highest at noon, and goes down in the evening. Then night comes.
hint: Start when the Sun first peeks over the ground.

q: Fish use gills to take in oxygen from the water.
why: Water moves over a fish's gills, which pull out oxygen. Sharks and most sea fish breathe this way.
hint: Fish cannot breathe air like we do.

q: Which tool tells you how hot or cold the air is?
why: A thermometer measures temperature. A ruler measures length, and a clock tells time.
hint: Weather reporters read this to tell the temperature.

q: Which of these is a gas?
why: A gas spreads out to fill whatever holds it. Milk is a liquid and ice is a solid.
hint: A gas has no shape of its own.

q: Put the life of a sea turtle in order, from the start.
why: Mother turtles lay eggs on sand. The babies hatch and race to the water, then grow up in the sea.
hint: Turtles begin life on land.

q: You toss a baseball straight up. What pulls it back down?
why: Gravity pulls everything toward the ground. Light and sound cannot pull on a ball.
hint: It is the same force that keeps you on the ground.

q: A butterfly can taste with its feet.
why: Butterflies have taste sensors on their feet. When one lands on a leaf, it can tell if the plant is good for its eggs.
hint: Think about where a butterfly lands.

q: Which of these does a plant use to make its food?
why: Plants use sunlight, water and air to make their own food. That is why most plants grow toward light.
hint: Plants lean toward a sunny window.

q: Which sea animal has a hard shell and walks sideways?
why: Crabs have hard shells and bent legs, so they scuttle sideways. Jellyfish have soft bodies, and dolphins swim.
hint: It lives near rocky shores and has claws.

q: A shadow forms when something blocks what?
why: A shadow is a dark spot where light cannot reach because an object is in the way.
hint: Shadows appear on sunny days.

q: What do we call the hot melted rock that flows out of a volcano?
why: Lava is melted rock from deep inside Earth. When it cools, it turns into hard rock again.
hint: It glows red and orange.

q: Which animal is a mammal that can truly fly?
why: Bats are the only mammals that really fly. Owls are birds and dragonflies are insects.
hint: It has fur and hunts at night.

q: What covers the outside of your whole body to protect it?
why: Skin is your body's biggest organ. It keeps germs out and water in. Bones and muscles are inside.
hint: You can see it and touch it.

q: Which planet is famous for its bright, wide rings?
why: Saturn's rings are made of ice and rock bits. Mars and Venus have no rings at all.
hint: It is a giant planet far from the Sun.

q: A shark can feel tiny ripples in the water made by a fish swimming nearby.
why: A row of sensors along a shark's sides, called the lateral line, feels ripples and tells it where prey is.
hint: Sharks hunt even in murky water.

q: Which kind of teeth would tell a scientist that a dinosaur ate meat?
why: Sharp, curved teeth cut through meat. Flat teeth grind leaves and other plants.
hint: Think about what teeth need to do to cut food.

q: Some dinosaurs sat on their nests of eggs, the way birds do.
why: Fossils show small dinosaurs curled over their eggs to keep them warm. Birds are the living relatives of dinosaurs.
hint: Think about what birds do with eggs.

q: Long ago, people connected stars into star pictures, like a hunter or a bear. What are these called?
why: A constellation is a pattern of stars that people see as a picture. Comets are icy space travelers.
hint: A word that starts with 'con' and ends in 'tion'.

q: Which tool shows which way the wind is blowing?
why: A weather vane swings to point where the wind comes from. A rain gauge measures rain.
hint: It often sits on top of a barn roof.

q: Which one shows a solid turning into a liquid?
why: Heat makes ice cream melt from solid to liquid. Boiling makes a gas, and frost is water turning into ice.
hint: Look for the one that starts out solid.
opts: Ice cream melting in the sun

q: A ramp makes it easier to move a heavy box up. Which simple machine is a ramp?
why: A slanted surface is called an inclined plane. A longer ramp is a gentler climb that needs less push.
hint: A ramp is a slanted slope.

q: Why does a catcher's mitt have thick padding?
why: Padding cushions the push of a fast pitch so it stings less. It does not change the ball's weight.
hint: Think about how a fast ball feels in your hand.
opts: It makes the ball a lot lighter
It softens the hit of a fast ball
It makes the ball bounce back faster

q: Your elbow and your knee are places where two bones meet and let you bend. What are they called?
why: Joints connect bones and let them move. Ribs are bones in your chest, and nerves carry messages.
hint: Without these, your legs would not bend.

q: Which part of a plant carries water up from the roots?
why: The stem works like a straw, moving water and minerals up to the leaves.
hint: Think of a straw standing in a cup.

q: An omnivore eats both plants and animals. Which one is an omnivore?
why: Bears eat berries, roots, fish and more. Cows eat only plants, and lions eat only meat.
hint: Look for the animal with the most varied menu.

q: How does a dolphin breathe air?
why: Dolphins are mammals with lungs. They pop up to the surface and breathe through a blowhole.
hint: Dolphins are mammals, not fish.
opts: Through a blowhole on its head

q: Which animal has fingerprints that look a lot like human fingerprints?
why: Koalas have tiny ridged fingerprints on their paws that are nearly like ours, even under a microscope.
hint: Think of an animal that grips branches with its paws.

q: Sunlight passes through raindrops and makes a rainbow. What does that show?
why: Raindrops split white sunlight into its separate colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet.
hint: The colors come from the light itself.
opts: Sunlight has many colors mixed in
Clouds save up colors for rainy days

q: A big drum and a small drum are hit. Which one makes the lower sound?
why: Bigger things wobble more slowly, and slow wobbles make low sounds. Small drums sound higher.
hint: Think of a deep thump versus a light tap.

q: Put these in order from smallest to biggest.
why: The Moon is smaller than Earth. Jupiter is much bigger than Earth, but the Sun is far bigger than Jupiter.
hint: Start with the one that circles Earth.

q: Earth goes around the Sun one time in about how many days?
why: One trip around the Sun takes about 365 days. That trip is what we call a year.
hint: It is the number of days in a year.

q: Warm air rises above cooler air, which helps hot air balloons float.
why: Warm air is lighter than the cool air around it, so it floats upward and lifts the balloon.
hint: Think about what a burner does to the air.

q: A model bridge falls down during a test. What should an engineer do next?
why: Engineers learn from failed tests. They fix the weak spot and try again until the design works.
hint: Failures give clues for a better design.
opts: Build the real one the exact same way
Decide that bridges can never work
Improve the weak part and test again

q: Which sea animal can make a pearl inside its shell?
why: An oyster coats a tiny grain with smooth layers, and over time it grows into a pearl.
hint: It has two shell halves that open and close.

q: A shark can smell a drop of blood in a huge amount of water. What does it smell with?
why: Water flows into a shark's nostrils, and a large part of its brain handles smell. Gills are for breathing.
hint: Smelling takes place near the front of the head.

q: Pteranodon soared over the dinosaurs' world. What kind of animal was it?
why: Pterosaurs like Pteranodon were flying reptiles. They lived alongside dinosaurs but were not dinosaurs.
hint: It had wings made of skin, not feathers.

q: Rockets burn fuel to fly. Why must a rocket carry its own oxygen into space?
why: Fire needs oxygen, and space has almost none. So rockets bring oxygen along with their fuel.
hint: Think about what a fire needs.
opts: Oxygen from Earth is too heavy to burn
The fuel would freeze without it
The engine would grow too hot
There is almost no air in space

q: An octopus has 8 arms. How many arms do 5 octopuses have in all?
why: Five octopuses with 8 arms each is 5 x 8 = 40 arms.
hint: Count in groups of eight.

q: A lizard warms up its body by resting in the sun.
why: Lizards cannot make much body heat, so they bask in sunshine to warm up, then hide or cool off when too hot.
hint: Think about where you see lizards in the morning.

q: What causes the loud boom of thunder?
why: Lightning heats the air so fast that it bursts outward, making a boom. Clouds do not crash together.
hint: Thunder always comes after something you see.
opts: Clouds bumping hard into each other

q: A magnet will NOT stick to which of these?
why: Magnets attract iron and steel. Aluminum, wood and plastic are not magnetic.
hint: Which one is not made of iron or steel?

q: An axe blade splits a log by pushing the wood apart. Which simple machine is the blade?
why: A wedge is thin on one edge and wide on the other, so it turns a push downward into a push outward.
hint: Think of the shape of a doorstop.

q: A hard swing sends a baseball much farther than a gentle tap. Why?
why: A harder hit gives the ball more speed and energy, so it flies farther. The ball's weight stays the same.
hint: Think about how big the push is.
opts: A bigger push gives it more speed
The ball weighs less after hard hits
A fast swing pushes air away first

q: Which part of your skeleton works like a cage to protect your heart and lungs?
why: Your ribs curve around your chest like a cage. The skull protects your brain, and the spine protects nerves.
hint: You can feel them on your chest.

q: Fast swimmers like sharks have smooth, pointed bodies. How does that shape help?
why: A smooth, tapered shape has less drag, so swimmers use less energy to move fast. Weight and floating are different.
hint: Think of how a pointed boat cuts through waves.
opts: It helps the animal float up
It makes the animal weigh less

q: Put the steps of how a fossil forms in order.
why: Burying an animal quickly protects its bones. Over millions of years minerals harden them into stone fossils.
hint: The fossil has to exist before anyone can find it.
opts: An animal dies and is buried
Sand and mud pile on top
Minerals slowly turn bone to rock

q: The whale shark is a fish, not a whale.
why: Whale sharks are sharks, so they are fish with gills. They get the name from their huge size.
hint: Does it have gills or lungs?

q: Leaves are green because they hold a green material that captures sunlight. What is it called?
why: Chlorophyll soaks up sunlight so a leaf can make food. In fall it breaks down, and other colors show.
hint: Its name starts with 'chloro,' which means green.

q: Parrotfish scrape algae off coral with hard, beak-like teeth. What does their waste become?
why: Parrotfish grind up bits of coral, and their waste becomes sand. One fish can make hundreds of pounds a year.
hint: Think of what a beach is made of.

q: A window is made of clear glass, and light passes straight through it. What is such a material called?
why: Transparent materials let light through so you can see clearly. Opaque materials block light completely.
hint: The word starts with 'trans,' meaning across.

q: You shout in a canyon and hear your voice again a moment later. What is this?
why: An echo is sound that bounces off a hard surface and comes back to you.
hint: The sound has to come back from somewhere.
opts: Sound turning into a flash of light
The wind repeating your own words
Sound bouncing off a hard surface
Your ears making a ringing noise

q: A first test version of a new invention is called a what?
why: Engineers build a prototype to test their idea, then improve it before making the final version.
hint: It is the first model made for testing.

q: Jellyfish have no brain, no heart and no bones.
why: A jellyfish is mostly water. A net of nerves senses the world, and the body moves water without a heart.
hint: Jellyfish are very simple animals.

q: During a solar eclipse, the Sun seems to vanish for a few minutes. What happens?
why: The Moon passes in front of the Sun and blocks its light. Earth's shadow causes a lunar eclipse instead.
hint: Think about what could block the Sun's light for a few minutes.
opts: Earth's shadow falls across the Sun
The Sun stops shining for a few minutes
A giant space cloud drifts past the Sun
The Moon moves between the Sun and Earth

q: A hammerhead shark sweeps its wide head back and forth over the sand. What is it most likely doing?
why: A hammerhead's wide head holds sensors spread far apart. Sweeping it over the sand helps it find stingrays buried below.
hint: Think about why wide-set sensors might help.
opts: Looking for a place to sleep

q: Fossil dinosaur poop is called a coprolite. What can scientists learn from it?
why: Coprolites can hold bits of bone, seeds, or plant fibers. Those clues show what a dinosaur had eaten.
hint: Think about what comes out after a meal.

q: About how many Earths could fit inside the Sun?
why: The Sun is enormous. Roughly 1.3 million Earths would fit inside it, even though it looks small from far away.
hint: The Sun makes Earth look like a tiny marble.

q: Suppose a coral reef grows 2 centimeters each year. How many centimeters does it grow in 15 years?
why: Growth adds up each year: 2 cm x 15 years = 30 cm. Real reefs grow slowly, so tall reefs are very old.
hint: Multiply the yearly growth by the years.

q: Which kind of rock forms when melted rock cools and hardens?
why: Igneous rock starts as lava or magma and hardens as it cools. Granite and basalt are examples.
hint: The name comes from a word for fire.

q: Which sentence is about climate rather than weather?
why: Weather is what the sky does on a given day. Climate is the usual pattern over many years.
hint: Climate describes what is true year after year.
opts: A heavy rain fell on town this morning
A strong wind blew all afternoon long
Snow fell on the hills late last night
This desert has hot, dry summers every year

q: You stir sugar into warm water and it seems to vanish. Where did the sugar go?
why: Sugar dissolves. Its tiny pieces mix evenly in the water. You can still taste it, so it is not gone.
hint: Taste the water and you can tell.
opts: It turned into more plain water
It mixed in as tiny, unseen bits
It was destroyed and is gone for good
It sank and hid at the bottom

q: A rope runs over a wheel at the top of a flagpole. What does this pulley help you do?
why: A fixed pulley changes the direction of your pull. It does not lower the weight or the effort needed.
hint: Think about which way your hands move.
opts: Pull down to raise the flag
Lift the flag with half the effort

q: A baseball rolls off a table. While it falls, it goes faster and faster. Why?
why: Gravity pulls the whole time the ball falls, so its speed keeps growing. The ball's weight stays the same.
hint: One force acts the entire fall.
opts: The air pushes it hard from above
The ball gets heavier as it falls

q: In bright light, the dark center of your eye gets smaller. What is that center called?
why: The pupil is the opening that lets light into the eye. The iris is the colored ring that makes it larger or smaller.
hint: It is a hole, not a ring.

q: Seaweed grows near the ocean's surface but not on the deep sea floor. Why?
why: Seaweed needs sunlight to make food, and sunlight fades with depth. Below a few hundred meters, it is dark.
hint: What do plants and seaweed need to make food?
opts: Deep water is far too salty
Waves are too strong down there
Hungry fish eat all the seaweed there

q: Put these in order of when they first appeared on Earth, earliest first.
why: Trilobites appeared over 500 million years ago, sharks about 450 million, dinosaurs about 230 million, and modern humans only about 300,000.
hint: Dinosaurs came long after the first sharks.

q: Sea otters sometimes hold paws while they sleep so they do not drift apart.
why: Sleeping otters float on the water and hold paws or wrap in kelp to stay together. Some otters do this in groups called rafts.
hint: Think about what floating animals worry about.

q: Earth's crust is broken into huge pieces that move very slowly. What are they called?
why: Tectonic plates drift a few centimeters a year. Where they bump or slide, earthquakes and volcanoes can happen.
hint: These pieces fit together like a giant puzzle.

q: A straw in a glass of water looks bent at the water's surface. Why?
why: Light changes direction when it moves between water and air, called refraction. The straw is still straight.
hint: Take the straw out and look again.
opts: Light bends between water and air
The straw really bends in water
The glass squeezes the straw sideways

q: You hit a drum harder. Why does it sound louder?
why: A harder hit makes bigger vibrations, and bigger vibrations make louder sound. Speed of sound stays the same.
hint: Think about how far the drum skin moves.
opts: The air around it gets thicker

q: An engineer wants a stronger bridge frame. Which shape adds the most strength?
why: Triangles do not bend out of shape easily, so bridges and towers use them everywhere.
hint: Look at the metal frames of big bridges.

q: Fungi and tiny bacteria break down fallen leaves on a forest floor. What does this do for the forest?
why: Decomposers turn dead leaves into nutrients that plants take up through their roots. Nothing is wasted in a healthy forest.
hint: Think about what happens to the leftovers of leaves.
opts: Gives trees new leaves right away
Makes the soil harder and drier

q: A flounder lies flat on the sandy sea floor and matches its colors. What does this help it do?
why: Camouflage hides the flounder from predators and from the small animals it hunts.
hint: Think about why a color match matters.
opts: Stay warm in the cold deep water
Blend in so it is hard to see
Swim much faster than any predator
Breathe more easily on the sand

q: Some dinosaurs were as small as a chicken.
why: Dinosaurs came in all sizes. Little ones like Compsognathus were about as big as a chicken.
hint: Not every dinosaur was giant.

q: Most fish float with a gas-filled swim bladder. Sharks have none. What helps a shark stay up?
why: Shark liver oil is lighter than seawater, so it gives some lift. Fins and a steady swim help too.
hint: Sharks have no air inside; think of oil floating on water.
opts: A big liver full of light oil
Warm blood that lifts the body

q: How do scientists work out how old a dinosaur fossil is?
why: Rock layers hold natural clocks: some minerals change at a steady pace. That tells the age of the fossils nearby.
hint: The rock tells time better than the bone.
opts: By dating the rock layers around it
By weighing the whole fossil today
By measuring how big it once grew
By counting the cracks in its bones

q: From Earth we always see the same side of the Moon. Why?
why: The Moon does spin. It turns exactly once while it orbits Earth once, so one face always points toward us.
hint: The Moon spins at a very particular rate.
opts: Its far side is always in Earth's shadow
It never spins on its axis
Clouds hide the far side from us
It spins once for each trip around Earth

q: Suppose only 10% of the energy in each step of a food chain passes to the next step. Plankton hold 10,000 units. How many units reach a shark that eats fish that eat the plankton?
why: Plankton hold 10,000, fish get 10% = 1,000, and the shark gets 10% of that = 100. Energy shrinks at each step.
hint: Take 10% twice.

q: Rising air cools. How does that help a cloud form?
why: Cool air holds less water vapor, so extra vapor condenses into droplets around bits of dust. Billions of drops make a cloud.
hint: Think about a cold glass on a warm day.
opts: Dust in the air turns into water
Water vapor turns into tiny droplets
Oxygen freezes into tiny ice crystals
Wind squeezes the rain out of the air

q: Which one is a chemical change, making a new substance?
why: Rust is a new substance, formed when iron meets oxygen and water. Melting, dissolving and tearing keep the same material.
hint: A chemical change cannot be easily undone.
opts: A nail rusting in the rain

q: In a wheelbarrow, where is the pivot point (fulcrum) of the lever?
why: The wheelbarrow turns around its wheel. The load sits between the wheel and your hands, which lift at the handles.
hint: The thing that stays in place when lifting is the pivot.
opts: In the middle of the load
At the front of the tray

q: A bat hits a ball with a strong push. What does the ball do to the bat?
why: Forces come in pairs of equal size, pointing opposite ways. That is why a hard hit can sting a batter's hands.
hint: Think about what a batter's hands feel.
opts: Pushes back with the same size force
Pushes back with a much smaller force
Pushes back with a much bigger force
Does not push back at all

q: Which part of your blood helps fight germs?
why: White blood cells find and attack germs. Red cells carry oxygen, and platelets plug cuts.
hint: The color tells you the cell type.

q: Which living things make most of the oxygen that comes from the ocean?
why: Phytoplankton use sunlight to make food and release oxygen. They make a huge share of the oxygen we breathe.
hint: The answer is small and drifts in sunlight.
opts: Giant kelp forests and nothing else

q: Put these layers of Earth's atmosphere in order, starting at the ground.
why: Weather happens in the troposphere. Higher up come the stratosphere, mesosphere, and thermosphere, where air is very thin.
hint: The name of the lowest layer starts with 'tropo.'

q: A bolt of lightning is hotter than the surface of the Sun.
why: Lightning heats air to about 30,000 degrees Celsius for a split second. The Sun's surface is only about 5,500.
hint: Lightning is brief but extremely hot.

q: Scientists find seashell fossils near the top of a tall mountain. What does this suggest?
why: Earth's plates push rock upward over millions of years. Mountains can lift old sea floor high into the sky.
hint: Think about where shellfish live and how land can move.
opts: Birds carried the shells up there
Heavy rain washed shells up the slope
Old sea floor was lifted up over time

q: A red shirt looks red in sunlight. What is happening to the light?
why: A thing's color is the light it bounces back to your eyes. A red shirt bounces red and soaks up other colors.
hint: The color you see is the light that bounces off.
opts: It makes red light inside itself
It absorbs red light and reflects the rest
It reflects red light and absorbs the rest

q: Put your ear on a railroad track and you may hear a far-off train sooner than through the air. Why?
why: Particles in solids are packed close together, so sound passes along faster than in air.
hint: Think about which material is more tightly packed.
opts: Sound moves faster in metal than air
Metal always makes sound louder than air
Trains make their sounds only in the metal
The air blocks all the sound of trains

q: A team makes a bike frame stronger with a new material, but the bike costs much more. What is this called?
why: Engineers weigh good and bad results of each design choice. Getting more of one thing often costs something else.
hint: You gain something and give up something else.

q: A desert fox has very large ears. How do they help it survive?
why: Blood flows through the thin, big ears and loses heat to the air, which helps keep the fox cool.
hint: Think about what a desert does to bodies.
opts: They let extra body heat escape
They store water for dry days

q: Leaves have tiny openings, mostly on the underside. What passes through them?
why: These openings, called stomata, let carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapor out.
hint: They work like tiny doors for gases.

q: Astronauts float inside the space station even though gravity still pulls on them. Why?
why: Gravity up there is still about 90% as strong. The station moves sideways so fast that it keeps falling around Earth.
hint: Gravity has not switched off.
opts: Gravity does not reach that far up
Both are falling around Earth together
Engines inside cancel out the gravity
The station sits above all of Earth's air

q: A day on Venus is longer than a year on Venus.
why: Venus spins very slowly: one turn takes about 243 Earth days, but one trip around the Sun takes only about 225.
hint: Venus is a very slow spinner.

q: Sharks have skeletons of cartilage, not bone. Which fish are their closest relatives?
why: Sharks, rays and skates all have cartilage skeletons and share a common ancestor. Tuna and eels have bony skeletons.
hint: Look for another flat or flexible-skeleton group.

q: Archaeopteryx had feathers and wings, but also teeth and a long bony tail. Why is this fossil so important?
why: Archaeopteryx mixes bird traits with dinosaur traits. That supports the idea that birds descended from dinosaurs.
hint: A mix of two animal groups.
opts: It has features of dinosaurs and birds
It proves that all dinosaurs could fly
It shows that birds lived before dinosaurs
It proves dinosaurs lived mostly in water

q: A star is 10 light-years away. What do you see when you look at it tonight?
why: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year. Light from that star left 10 years ago, so you see its past.
hint: Light takes time to travel across space.
opts: The star as it is right now
The star as it was 10 days ago
The star as it was 10 years ago

q: Earth makes one full turn, 360 degrees, in 24 hours. How many degrees does it turn in 1 hour?
why: 360 divided by 24 equals 15. This is why time zones are about 15 degrees wide.
hint: Divide the full turn by the number of hours.

q: A hurricane weakens fast when it moves over land. Why?
why: Hurricanes get energy from warm ocean water. Over land, that supply is cut off, and rubbing against land slows the winds.
hint: What is the storm's energy source?
opts: Land has far too much cool wind
It loses the warm ocean that feeds it
Mountains tear it into small pieces
Land makes the air press down harder

q: A solid steel nail sinks, yet a huge steel ship floats. Why?
why: A ship's hollow shape makes its overall density less than water. It pushes aside water equal to its weight, so it floats.
hint: Think about the whole ship's shape, not just its metal.
opts: Ship steel is a lighter kind of steel
The engine pushes it up from below
Large objects feel less of gravity's pull
Its hollow shape pushes aside lots of water

q: A gear with 10 teeth drives a gear with 40 teeth. How many turns of the small gear make the big gear turn exactly once?
why: Each turn of the small gear moves 10 teeth, so it takes 40 divided by 10 = 4 turns to move all 40 teeth.
hint: Count how many teeth need to pass by.

q: A pitched ball's motion energy depends on its speed squared. If a pitch is twice as fast, its motion energy becomes how many times bigger?
why: Doubling the speed multiplies the speed squared by 2 x 2 = 4. That is why fast pitches are so much harder to catch.
hint: Square the number 2.

q: Why can two eyes judge distance better than one eye?
why: The brain compares two slightly different views to work out how far away things are. Close one eye and it is harder.
hint: Your eyes are a few centimeters apart.
opts: Each eye sees from a different spot
Two eyes take in twice as much light
One eye is always closed inside the brain
Each eye sees a different color of light

q: A deep-sea anglerfish dangles a glowing lure. How is the light made?
why: This is bioluminescence. Chemicals react and give off light without heat. It can lure small prey in the dark.
hint: Light can come from chemistry, not only from heat or sunlight.
opts: By soaking up sunlight all day
By electric sparks like a tiny battery
By chemical reactions in living cells

q: Put the path of a sound through your ear in order.
why: Sound shakes the eardrum, tiny bones pass the shaking inward, and nerves turn it into signals your brain understands.
hint: The eardrum is the first thing to wiggle.
opts: Sound waves enter the ear canal
Tiny bones pass on the shaking

q: A metal spoon feels colder than a wooden spoon in the same room because the metal really is colder.
why: Both are the same temperature as the room. Metal pulls heat out of your hand faster, so it feels colder.
hint: Both spoons have sat in the same room.

q: Scientists study air bubbles trapped in very old polar ice. What can the bubbles show them?
why: Snow packs down into ice and traps bubbles of the air from that time. Deeper ice holds older air.
hint: The bubbles were sealed in when the snow fell.
opts: What Earth's air was like long ago
Which animals lived in the ice
How many storms struck last year

q: You stand 2 meters in front of a flat mirror. How many meters away from you does your reflection seem to be?
why: Your reflection seems to be as far behind the mirror as you are in front: 2 m + 2 m = 4 m from you.
hint: The reflection is behind the mirror.

q: An ambulance siren sounds higher as it comes toward you and lower as it drives away. Why?
why: Moving toward you squeezes the waves closer together, giving a higher pitch. Moving away spreads them out.
hint: The truck moves while the sound is made.
opts: The siren changes its own tune on purpose
Sound travels faster as the truck leaves

q: A tall, narrow block tower and a short, wide one are pushed. Why is the wide, low tower harder to tip?
why: A low center of gravity above a wide base keeps the tower balanced, so a tip needs a larger push.
hint: Think about where the weight is and what it stands on.
opts: It has far fewer blocks in the tower
Its blocks are all heavier on one side
Its weight sits lower over a wider base
Wind cannot touch a wide, low tower

q: A harmless hoverfly has yellow and black stripes like a stinging wasp. What is this trick called?
why: In mimicry, one animal looks like another that predators avoid. Camouflage blends into the background instead.
hint: It copies another animal's look.

q: A tiny seed grows into a tree that weighs tons. Where do the carbon atoms in its wood come from?
why: Leaves take in carbon dioxide from the air and build it into sugars and wood. Sunlight gives energy, not atoms.
hint: Trees build wood from a gas.

q: Why is a black hole black?
why: A black hole packs huge mass into a tiny space. Gravity near it is so strong that even light cannot get out.
hint: Think about what escapes from strong gravity.
opts: Even light cannot escape its gravity
It is wrapped in thick black dust clouds
It is too cold to give off light
It is an empty hole with no mass

q: Sharks lived on Earth before the first trees did.
why: Sharks swam in oceans more than 400 million years ago. The first trees appeared about 385 million years ago.
hint: Sharks have been around for a very long time.
